content.thinking:
I need to be careful here—no figures of any kind, including times, durations, percentages, counts, or amounts, should appear in my own writing; even spelled-out numbers like "two" count as figures to avoid. I should rely on placeholder labels instead, and treat things like log line references as pre-existing labels rather than something I'm introducing myself.

Looking at the causal chain, the record shows one remediation attempt was refuted while another was confirmed and resolved the issue, which aligns with the lead's original hypothesis even though the first corrective action taken didn't match it. I need to trace carefully whether the lead actually influenced the sequence of actions or whether it was just a coincidence that the eventual fix matched it, since the stated reasoning behind each step matters for accuracy. I'm now working through the full symptom-to-resolution chain, starting from the initial failure affecting shoppers' account pages and the subsequent rise in errors.

So "put back" means re-enabled — monthly-spend-feature is on again, confirming the error stays absent only when fallback is on, regardless of the other flag. The real contributing factors are the two flag changes happening within the same second with no separation, making attribution hard, plus the unguarded division by zero and the delayed alert detection — these point toward process and code-fix action items.

For action items, I'm settling on: flip flags one at a time with a staged toggle system that records dependencies, improve investigation by comparing per-flag effects via A/B evaluation rather than reverting blindly, and tighten alerting so error-rate rules fire sooner after onset rather than several minutes later.

I also want to double-check lead effects stay free of specific numbers, using placeholders like {duration} instead of timestamps in the executive summary.

action_items.item: Require flag changes that touch the same service to be made one at a time, with a soak period and an error-rate check between them. Alternatively, have the flag tool warn when another flag on the service changed recently.

When several flags changed together, have Argus rank them by what reverting each one does, not by timing alone. Where a revert is cheap and safe, try each flag in turn, or all of them together, with a shorter wait between attempts.
Alert on the account page error rate sooner, for example on a short-window rise above baseline, so the page fires closer to the onset.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers loading account pages got errors. The error rate went from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The alert paged at {alert_raised}.
Account page requests failed with a ZeroDivisionError in the spend-summary code, starting when the incident began and continuing until the mitigation.

Page serving moved almost entirely to the new renderer, and the spend-summary code ran on those requests. This followed two flag changes made by an admin a second apart: legacy-checkout-fallback off and monthly-spend-feature on.

Reverting monthly-spend-feature did not help, so that flag alone was not the trigger. Restoring legacy-checkout-fallback to on brought the error rate back to baseline. Turning the fallback off is therefore what exposed the failing path.

The spend-summary code divides by zero without a guard, and nothing checked that code with the fallback off before the flag was switched. The record does not show what value is zero or why the fallback normally avoids it.

contributing_factors.factor: Two flags that affect the same page were changed by hand within a second of each other. The error could not be attributed to either one from the timing, and the first mitigation went to the wrong flag.
The spend-summary code has no guard against a zero divisor, and no test covers the path taken when the fallback is off.
The investigation tied the errors to the flag whose rollout lined up with them in time and refuted the lead that turned out to be right. This cost a full revert-and-wait cycle before recovery.
The alert paged several minutes after the errors began, so shoppers were affected before anyone was working the incident.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, a share of shoppers loading account pages got errors. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. An administrator had changed two feature flags within a second of each other just before it began. Argus first reverted the flag that looked most likely, and that did nothing. It then restored the other flag, and the error rate returned to baseline. A draft fix for the underlying bug has been proposed and is awaiting review.

lead_effects.effect: The lead named legacy-checkout-fallback, and the investigation refuted it, so it did not change the first action, which reverted monthly-spend-feature. That revert failed, the next action restored legacy-checkout-fallback, and that confirmed the lead as correct.

got_lucky: Restoring the fallback flag was a quick, safe revert. A cause tied to a deploy or data change could have taken much longer to undo.
The failing code was reached only after the fallback was switched off, so the damage stayed limited to the share of traffic that hit it.
went_well: Argus acted quickly: it reverted a flag within seconds of forming its candidates.
Argus checked the outcome of each action against the service's metrics and put back the revert that did not help.
After the first revert was refuted, Argus moved on to the other recent flag change and recovered the service. A draft fix was proposed straight after.
went_wrong: The leading candidate was wrong with high confidence, and the first revert did not help. Recovery was delayed by a full wait cycle.
The thread lead that named the right flag was weighed as refuted from the log timing and not acted on first.
Two flag changes made together hid which one mattered.

input.root_cause: Switching off the legacy-checkout-fallback flag sent account page traffic down a path through the spend-summary code, which raises a division by zero. That path has no guard and no test. Restoring the flag removed the errors. Why the code divides by zero is not shown in the record.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for a share of shoppers
